newsitem.title: UK: EMU on track for 1999, with Ireland & Finland.
newsitem.headline: EMU on track for 1999, with Ireland & Finland.

text.p: European economic and monetary union (EMU) is virtually certain to go ahead as scheduled in January 1999, with Ireland and Finland joining six "core" countries, a Reuters survey showed on Thursday.
The poll of 36 think-tanks and economists across Europe predicted that on average, the single currency was 80 percent likely to happen in some form on the set launch date.

"For political and economic reasons EMU (on time) is now a near certainty. It would be economically unsound to delay and politically, would require changes in the Maastricht treaty," Copenhagen University economics Professor Niels Thygesen said.
Reuters surveyed opinion in all 15 European Union countries except Luxembourg in the first of a series of regular monthly surveys on the structure of EMU. Switzerland was also included.
All the panelists said EMU will begin with Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.

But some of the key candidates -- Italy, Portugal, Spain and Britain -- are expected to stand aside or fail to qualify, the survey showed. Fewer than 10 percent of respondents expect these four countries to be in the first wave.

"The six core countries are very much integrated from an economic point of view," said Brian Venables, senior bond strategist at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in the Netherlands. "They have stable exchange and interest rates and the political will, which means they can comfortably move forward with EMU".
Finland -- which joined Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) two weeks ago -- should also make the grade, according to 83 percent of respondents.

An overwhelming ninety-two percent said Ireland would also join EMU in 1999, although some analysts note this cannot be considered a fait accompli because of the proximity of Britain, which is wavering on the issue.
Maastricht guidelines state that in order to qualify for EMU, a country's debt should be no more than 60 percent of GDP and its budget deficit no more than three percent of GDP.

Long term interest rates should not be more than two percentage points higher than the country with the lowest inflation, while inflation itself should be within 1.5 percent of the average of the three best price performers in the union.
Finally, the member currency should have been within "normal bands' of the ERM for two years prior to the start of EMU.
But all these criteria are subject to interpretation.
"Even strict adherence to the criteria still gives countries plenty of lee-way," one London-based EMU expert said.
Italy and Spain have recently surprised financial markets with their willingness to rein in spending as part of their drive to meet the tough EMU criteria.

But some survey respondents warned that uncertainty over interpretation of the criteria could scupper EMU's timetable, while concern remains that governments will massage budget balances rather than strive for long-term stability.
"If necessary, politicians can fulfil the letter of the law in Maastricht if not the spirit of the Treaty," said Venables.

France came under fire after using some of the proceeds from the sale of 20 percent of its state-owned telecommunications firm to cut next year's budget deficit. The Maastricht Treaty states that privatisation revenues cannot be used in this way.

Stephen King, chief European economist at HSBC James Capel in London, warned this deal could "open the back door for other countries to join". There would be political problems if France was included in the launch of a single currency while countries like Italy and Spain were left out, he said.

"The simplest (solution) of all would be to delay rather than have a huge argument next year about who should be in and who should be out and how all the convergence criteria have been interpreted," he said. King, a sceptic, thinks the chances of EMU going ahead on time could be as low as 50 percent.
Rob Hayward, economic advisor at Bank America in London, also sees a risk in applying flexible policy selectively.
"It's difficult for German politicians to sell monetary union if people become convinced they're giving up the Deutschemark for some wishy-washy euro-currency," he said.
The survey shows that although Denmark and Sweden are likely to meet convergence criteria, both countries are likely to opt out. Denmark's public has rejected joining EMU in a referendum.
Britain, still dithering ahead of national elections expected around May 1997, is also likely to opt out. None of the experts polled thought Greece would join in the first phase.
